title: Thirst, weight loss and vomiting in a 19-year-old
opening_brief:
You are a medical student in the emergency department.

A 19-year-old college student has been brought in by a friend with two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He looks unwell and is breathing heavily.

Assess him, decide what you need at the bedside, and justify your reasoning.

patient.name: Arjun Pillai
patient.background: Lives in a college hostel. Normally fit, plays football.

persona.speech_style: Tired, speaks in short phrases because he is breathing deeply.
knows_not: what the doctors are testing his urine for
whether anyone in the family has a sugar problem, beyond a vague memory
quirks: Attributes everything to food poisoning from the hostel mess.

chief_complaint: vomiting and abdominal pain for two days

present_illness.onset: Vomiting started two days ago. But he has felt unwell for about three weeks.
present_illness.site: Pain all over the abdomen, no particular spot.
present_illness.duration: Two days of vomiting; three weeks of feeling generally unwell.
present_illness.severity: Pain 5 out of 10. The tiredness is what bothers him most.
present_illness.timing: Continuous over the last two days.
associated: extremely thirsty for the last three weeks, finishing several bottles of water a day
passing urine very often, including getting up four or five times at night
lost weight — trousers are loose, thinks about 6 kg in a month
very tired, stopped going to football practice
present_illness.progression: The thirst and urination have been getting worse for three weeks; the vomiting and breathlessness started in the last two days.

past_medical: Had a bad throat infection about six weeks ago that settled on its own
Says nobody has ever told him he has a sugar problem, and he has no asthma
medications: Took an antacid and a paracetamol for the stomach pain
family: An aunt on his mother's side takes injections every day, he thinks for her sugar
social: Drinks alcohol very occasionally at parties, none in the last month
Eats hostel food, has not been eating much for two days
review_of_systems_positive: mouth feels dry all the time
review_of_systems_negative: no fever that he has measured

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Temperature 37.1 C. Pulse 124/min. BP 96/58 mmHg. Respiratory rate 30/min, deep and sighing. SpO2 99% on room air.

examination.label: Capillary blood glucose
examination.result: HI on the glucometer (above the readable range of 500 mg/dL).

examination.label: General examination
examination.result: Thin, unwell, visibly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. Sweet acetone smell on the breath. No pallor, no icterus, no rash, no lymphadenopathy.

examination.label: Pattern of breathing
examination.result: Deep, laboured, regular sighing respiration — Kussmaul breathing. No use of accessory muscles for airway obstruction, no wheeze.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.result: Chest clear, equal air entry, no crackles, no wheeze.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Sinus tachycardia. Heart sounds normal. JVP low. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Peripheries cool.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.result: Mild generalised tenderness with no guarding or rigidity. Bowel sounds present. No organomegaly, no mass. No rebound.

examination.label: Conscious level and neurological examination
examination.result: GCS 15, alert and fully oriented but tired. No focal deficit. No neck stiffness.

examination.label: Foot and skin examination for a source of infection
examination.result: No ulcer, no cellulitis, no abscess, no dental infection. Skin intact.

investigations.label: Venous or arterial blood gas
investigations.result: pH 7.11, pCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 7 mEq/L, base excess -21, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Anion gap 26 mEq/L.

investigations.label: Serum electrolytes and renal function
investigations.result: Sodium 129 mEq/L (corrected for glucose: 137). Potassium 5.4 mEq/L. Chloride 96. Bicarbonate 7 mEq/L. Urea 62 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Anion gap 26.

investigations.label: Urine dipstick
investigations.result: Ketones 4+, glucose 4+, protein trace, no nitrites, no leucocytes, no blood.

investigations.label: Complete blood count
investigations.result: Hb 15.6 g/dL (haemoconcentrated). WBC 16,800/uL with neutrophilia — common in ketoacidosis without infection. Platelets 310,000/uL.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia at 122/min. Tall peaked T waves in the precordial leads consistent with hyperkalaemia. No ischaemic changes.

investigations.label: HbA1c
investigations.result: 12.8% — confirming several months of hyperglycaemia rather than an acute stress response.

investigations.label: Serum phosphate and magnesium
investigations.result: Phosphate 4.6 mg/dL (will fall with treatment). Magnesium 2.0 mg/dL.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Clear lung fields. No consolidation. Normal heart size.

investigations.label: Anti-GAD and islet autoantibodies, C-peptide
investigations.result: Anti-GAD strongly positive. Anti-IA2 positive. C-peptide low at 0.2 ng/mL — confirming type 1 diabetes.

investigations.label: Serum lipase
investigations.result: Mildly raised at 92 U/L (under three times the upper limit).
investigations.note: Lipase is often mildly raised in ketoacidosis without pancreatitis. Ordering it is reasonable, but do not let a mild rise derail the diagnosis.

investigations.label: CT abdomen
investigations.note: The abdominal pain of ketoacidosis resolves with treatment. Imaging before correcting the metabolic derangement wastes time and contrast in a dehydrated patient.

differentials.why: The diagnostic triad is complete: glucose 612 mg/dL, ketones 5.8 mmol/L with 4+ on urine dipstick, and pH 7.11 with bicarbonate 7 and a raised anion gap.

Three weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 6 kg weight loss in a lean 19-year-old, HbA1c 12.8%, positive anti-GAD and low C-peptide. Naming the underlying disease, not just the acute complication, is required.

The other hyperglycaemic emergency, but it occurs in older type 2 patients with far higher glucose, minimal ketones and no acidosis. Distinguishing them matters because the fluid and insulin strategies differ.

Tachycardia, hypotension, a raised white count and an acidosis all fit. Excluded by a lactate of 1.4, ketones of 5.8 and no source — but a precipitating infection must always be sought in ketoacidosis.

Ketoacidosis frequently presents with abdominal pain and a raised white count and is misdiagnosed as a surgical abdomen. Here there is no guarding, no rigidity and no rebound, and the pain settles with treatment.
Other causes of a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperventilation, worth considering when ketones are negative. Not the case here.
The patient's own explanation. It does not cause a glucose of 612, ketonuria, Kussmaul breathing or three weeks of polyuria and weight loss.
Produces mild ketosis with normal or low glucose and rarely a pH below 7.3.

final_diagnosis: Diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose 612 mg/dL, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, pH 7.11, bicarbonate 7, anion gap 26) as the first presentation of type 1 diabetes mellitus, with hypovolaemia, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, no identified precipitating infection
diagnosis_reasoning: Three weeks of osmotic symptoms — polyuria, polydipsia and 6 kg of weight loss in a lean adolescent — establish undiagnosed diabetes. The acute deterioration with vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath is decompensation into ketoacidosis, confirmed by all three diagnostic criteria. HbA1c 12.8% shows this is not stress hyperglycaemia, and positive anti-GAD with a low C-peptide establishes type 1 rather than type 2. The abdominal pain and neutrophilia are consequences of the ketoacidosis, not evidence of a second illness; cultures and imaging found no precipitant, so the likely trigger is simply the natural progression of untreated beta-cell failure, possibly following the viral illness six weeks ago.

history.label: Polyuria, nocturia and thirst
history.teaching_note: The osmotic symptoms are the history that makes this diagnosis. Anchoring on 'vomiting for two days' and never asking about the preceding weeks is the trap.

history.label: Weight loss
history.teaching_note: Weight loss with polyuria in a young person is type 1 diabetes until proved otherwise.

history.label: Duration and time course of the whole illness
history.teaching_note: Explicitly asking whether anything preceded the acute illness is what uncovers the three-week prodrome.

history.label: Vomiting and oral intake
history.teaching_note: Determines the degree of fluid deficit and whether oral treatment is even possible.

history.label: Search for a precipitating illness
history.teaching_note: Every episode of ketoacidosis needs a precipitant sought — infection, missed insulin, myocardial infarction or a new diagnosis.

history.label: Family history of diabetes and autoimmune disease
history.teaching_note: Type 1 diabetes clusters with other autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid and coeliac.

history.label: Visual blurring
history.teaching_note: Osmotic lens changes are a common and reversible early symptom of hyperglycaemia.

history.label: Drug and substance history
history.teaching_note: Steroids, alcohol and toxic ingestions all feature in the differential of an anion-gap acidosis.

history.label: Character of the abdominal pain
history.teaching_note: Diffuse pain without localisation or peritonism argues against a surgical cause.

history.label: Known diabetes and insulin use
history.teaching_note: In a known diabetic, missed insulin doses are the commonest precipitant.

examination.label: Bedside capillary glucose
examination.teaching_note: Ten seconds, and it makes the diagnosis. There is no excuse for not doing it in any acutely unwell patient.

examination.label: Bedside capillary or urine ketones
examination.teaching_note: Distinguishes ketoacidosis from a hyperosmolar state and from simple hyperglycaemia.

examination.label: Vital signs including respiratory rate
examination.teaching_note: A respiratory rate of 30 in a patient with no chest signs should immediately raise metabolic acidosis.

examination.label: Assessment of hydration and perfusion
examination.teaching_note: The fluid deficit in ketoacidosis is typically 5 to 8 litres and drives the first hour of management.

examination.label: Pattern of breathing and breath odour
examination.teaching_note: Kussmaul respiration and ketotic breath are classic bedside signs that students read about and then forget to look for.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.teaching_note: Distinguishing the diffuse pain of ketoacidosis from true peritonism prevents an unnecessary laparotomy.

examination.label: Conscious level
examination.teaching_note: A falling conscious level in ketoacidosis signals severity and the risk of cerebral oedema, especially in the young.

examination.label: Examination for a source of infection
examination.teaching_note: The precipitant is often a small, easily overlooked infection.

investigations.label: Blood gas with pH and bicarbonate
investigations.teaching_note: The third leg of the diagnostic triad and the marker of severity. A venous gas is sufficient — an arterial sample is rarely necessary.

investigations.label: Blood or urine ketones
investigations.teaching_note: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is preferred: urine dipsticks measure acetoacetate and can look falsely reassuring early and falsely persistent late.

investigations.label: Electrolytes, renal function and anion gap
investigations.teaching_note: Potassium governs everything: total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level is high, and insulin will drive it down fast.

investigations.label: Laboratory plasma glucose
investigations.teaching_note: Needed because the glucometer only reads 'HI' above its range.

investigations.label: ECG
investigations.teaching_note: Shows hyperkalaemic changes and screens for a silent myocardial infarction as a precipitant.

investigations.label: Complete blood count
investigations.teaching_note: Interpret with care — a neutrophilia is expected in ketoacidosis and does not by itself indicate infection.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray, blood and urine cultures
investigations.teaching_note: A precipitant should be actively looked for in every case.

investigations.label: HbA1c
investigations.teaching_note: Separates a new chronic diagnosis from acute stress hyperglycaemia.

investigations.label: Islet autoantibodies and C-peptide
investigations.teaching_note: Confirms type 1 and commits the patient to lifelong insulin — an important conversation to get right at diagnosis.

hints: The vomiting is two days old, but ask yourself what he told you about the previous three weeks.
He is breathing deeply with a clear chest and normal saturations. What is the body compensating for, and what would you measure at the bedside to find out?
Review the metabolic emergencies that produce a raised anion gap acidosis with a very high blood sugar, and how the two hyperglycaemic emergencies differ from each other.
teaching_points: Check a capillary glucose in every acutely unwell patient. It takes seconds and here it is the whole diagnosis.
Diabetic ketoacidosis is defined by all three of: hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), ketonaemia, and metabolic acidosis. Any one alone is not enough.
Deep sighing breathing with a clear chest and normal saturations means metabolic acidosis, not a respiratory problem.
Abdominal pain and a neutrophilia are common features of ketoacidosis itself. Do not rush to a surgical diagnosis before the metabolic state is corrected.
Serum potassium is usually high on arrival while total body potassium is profoundly depleted. Insulin without potassium replacement can be fatal.
Fluid first, then insulin. Always look for a precipitant.
Do not measure a glucose and stop there — the underlying question is what type of diabetes this is.
